title: Why Oliver's band broke up, and Oliver's later years
summary: The recording substitution row with Johnny Dodds split the band, Oliver's later bands were outplayed by Young's band at the Wisconsin Roof, and Jackson met him later in Galveston.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: No, well that's what happened. Well Lee was playing there, he was playing there with Rudy and Nichols and his boys, they were playing together there. And then Joe was on the drums. And Joe lived right there at 31st Estate. Joe was teaching this boy, this Italian boy, I call his name. Penico? Yeah, he was teaching Penico. Yeah, he was teaching Penico. And Joe, he'd be taking a whole lot of time up with them young musicians, time with him, I mean as far as teaching them and telling them this and telling them that and telling them this. Now Joe, what broke up there, what caused the downfall of Joe Oliver's band was Joe had a contract to record for Jeanette. And Joe decided to do some recording for Victor or one of those others. And what they told Joe says, well anybody can tell that's your band, says any way that you could make some substitution so that it would sound a bit different. So Joe didn't want to get in trouble with Jeanette either, so he substituted, asking for Dutre and noon for Johnny Dodds. That caused the trouble. Well they didn't find out immediately. It may have been two or three when the records were released. Then they heard the records and that's when the trouble comes. So Johnny pulls away from Joe and goes over down Rush Street. I played there once with him. And Joe gets Bob Shottley, Tick Gray, the fellas, and goes in the plantation. He plays at the Lincoln Garden or Royal Garden, they change the name you know once or twice.
Oh Tick Gray, is that any relation to the union president?
No, no relation at all. Is he from Chicago or New Orleans?

And Bob Shottley, he's from St. Louis, he played with Charlie Creston. He's playing now. Yeah, yeah. Well that's about the same Bob Shottley. So he gets that band and Ori on the trombone and they play the plantation. Well Johnny and Dutre is playing with Dominic. Dominic's playing trumpet on down Rush with Baby Dodds. So that caused the split in the band. So Joe, after there, he leaves the plantation. In the meantime, Louie's in New York, Joe goes to New York and forms a band. He fooled around the Middle West a while with Red Allen playing with him and over there. They came and played against us with Bunny Young's band at the Wisconsin Roof. But there wasn't no match for us because they wasn't together. They were a band five years ago with three good arrangements and most of the bands stood at the Marquette University branch. You see I was studying myself to do harmony in theory myself. And we were on the job every night. Now maybe the old Joe Alva band would have given us fits, but not that Joe Alva band except for Henry Allen. And so there was some talk about him trying to get the job but it just blew him out of there. We had Randolph there, it wasn't Randolph. You know that boy played a whole lot of horn. If he was from St. Louis, where are we from? That boy, and it just blew him out of there. And Joe, Joe was beginning to have him in trouble with his teeth anyhow. And so we just blew him on, there was nothing. There was a whole lot of bands that had been up there that was better than that, we just blew him out of there. And so then Joe goes on out east and he flew around out there. Well the next time I saw Joe I stand by this hotel over there at South Park in the Ritz. By the Ritz. And he came through there and he lost quite a bit of weight. Then I meet him, when I'm with Louis Armstrong, I meet him down in Galveston. He still had a band. Well I guess you read about the trouble he had about the buses. Well he was having his telephone. He was on his way out. He was on his way out then. Yeah. He was on his way out then. But he was telling me, he heard us tell me, he says, boy you sure did come along on the trombone. You sure did come along on the trombone. He says, I didn't think he'd ever make it. I stumbled around a long time Bill, but things had just begun to come to me. The first thing, I didn't want to play the trombone. See I wanted to like, I was, he said, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew, whew. I can't whistle and say it like I used to. But I could whistle, I could go, whew, you know, things like that.
